newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection under way in Florida tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection under way in Florida tobacco case.

text.p: Jury selection began Monday in a landmark secondhand-smoke lawsuit by airline flight attendants against the tobacco industry after the judge refused to decertify the case's class-action status.

The screening of the panel of potential jurors who will hear the historic lawsuit -- the first class action and first secondhand-smoke case against the tobacco industry to go to trial -- began slowly.
Rival attorneys agreed that a long-time smoker impatient with restrictions on smoking in public should not be a juror in the $5 billion case against nine cigarette companies.

The suit, known as Broin v Philip Morris et al, was filed on behalf of some 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants who say they contracted a variety of maladies, including lung cancer, from breathing cigarette smoke on U.S.-based passenger jets.

Judge Robert Kaye also refused the companies' motion to deny the flight attendants' request for punitive damages and denied the industry's request for a summary judgment on allegations that the companies committed fraud and conspiracy.
Kaye ruled on those issues on Friday but the rulings were released only on Monday.

Tobacco stocks were lower after the rulings. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. was down $1.25 to $42.75 a share, and RJR Nabsico Holdings Corp. was down 62.5 cents at $31.75 a share, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
The trial began as the White House said a negotiated settlement between state attorneys general and the tobacco industry seemed a long way off.

Spokesman Mike McCurry said the White House was monitoring negotiations but indicated a deal would need to ensure "the best possible public health outcome" and might not immediately win White House approval.

The trial began with industry attorneys and Susan and Stanley Rosenblatt, the husband-and-wife team representing the plaintiffs, vying over comments to the media and how the hundreds of potential jurors expected to be screened for the panel should be questioned.
"We ask that the court issue a gag order directing counsel on both sides not to speak to the press until the trial is over," Philip Morris attorney David Hardy said.
Kaye did not immediately rule on the request. To date, he has limited access to some court documents and asked attorneys to be "circumspect" in talking to the press.

The judge, who had expressed concern about losing too many jurors during a trial expected to last several weeks, ordered 18 chairs be made ready for what was expected to be a panel of six jurors and as many as 12 alternates.

In other rulings since Friday, Kaye dismissed two of the defendants in the case, Dosal Tobacco Co., a small family-owned cigarette maker in Opa-locka, Fla., and United States Tobacco Co., a unit of UST Co. Inc., the largest seller of snuff and chewing tobacco. The ruling left nine defendants.
Lead plaintiff Norma Broin attended the first day of the trial, sitting in the courtroom's front row with Patty Young, another plaintiff.
Broin, who was using vacation time from her American Airlines flight attendant's job to be at the trial, said she was "ecstatic" to see the case, which was filed in 1991, finally making it to court.

Broin, 42, lost part of a lung several years ago to surgery for cancer, now in remission. Young, 50, who was a leader of flight attendants' effort to ban smoking on most U.S. flights, suffers from asthma, chronic bronchitis and other ailments she attributes to breathing secondhand smoke.
"I'm overwhelmed with happiness that something's finally happening here," Young said.

Only six potential jurors were questioned before a lunch break. More than 200 others were standing by for questioning. Kaye released a second possible juror, an attorney with a one-man practice, because of potential hardship.

The judge refused a request by attorney Susan Roseblatt to dismiss two potential women jurors. One said the flight attendants should have found other work to avoid secondhand smoke, while the other wavered over whether she would be able to find the tobacco companies liable for the alleged injuries.
Another juror both sides immediately agreed should be sent home described himself as a heavy smoker for decades and said, "I'm a smoker and my health is the same as it was when I started smoking."
